text_html: A 20-year-old man comes to the office because of a 4-year history of episodes of recurrent, painful ulcers in the mouth and groin. He has had oral ulcers approximately three to four times yearly and ulcers on the scrotum less frequently. Physical examination shows ulcerations along the buccal mucosa and similar lesions on the scrotum with scarring. He also has bilateral painful erythematous nodules on the shins. There are nail fold capillary abnormalities on the fingers. Serologic testing is negative for antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_html:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with a 4-year history of mouth and groin ulcers along with painful nodules on his shins, which is consistent with Behçet syndrome. The diagnosis is further supported by laboratory studies that are negative for other common rheumatologic diseases, as Behçet syndrome is a clinical diagnosis that involves excluding other diagnoses.

Evaluation: Behçet syndrome is a systemic vasculitis that classically presents with recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and ocular and cutaneous manifestations. Behçet syndrome results from immune dysregulation, which leads to expansion of Th1 and Th17 cells with decreased regulatory T lymphocytes. This aberrancy results in neutrophilic infiltration, which causes vasculitis.

Definition: Behçet syndrome is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorder characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, eye inflammation (uveitis), and skin lesions, caused by an abnormal immune response in genetically predisposed individuals. It is a type of systemic vasculitis that can affect blood vessels of all sizes and may involve the joints, nervous system, and gastrointestinal tract. The gold standard for diagnosis of Behçet syndrome is clinical manifestations of recurrent oral ulceration plus two of: recurrent genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions, or positive pathergy test. Diagnosis of Behçet syndrome also requires exclusion of other conditions with similar presentations.

Prevention: There are not any known prevention strategies for Behçet syndrome.

Treatment: Treatment for Behçet syndrome varies by severity. In moderate to severe cases, therapy includes immunosuppressants such as high-dose corticosteroids and biologic agents such as infliximab or adalimumab.

Differential: This patient's differential is initially broad and includes diagnoses such as inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and herpes simplex virus. However, the differential narrows when the patient is found to have groin ulcers and erythematous nodules on his shins along with negative serologic testing.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Choice B: Churg-Strauss syndrome is incorrect. Churg-Strauss syndrome is a small-to-medium vessel vasculitis that is characterized by asthma, eosinophilia, and vasculitis affecting other organs.

Choice C: Goodpasture syndrome is incorrect. Goodpasture syndrome is an autoimmune disease characterized by anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies that cause rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.

Choice D: Lofgren syndrome is incorrect. Lofgren syndrome is a form of acute sarcoidosis that presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, and polyarthritis.

Choice E: Sjögren syndrome is incorrect. Sjögren syndrome is a chronic autoimmune disease that is characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands, which most often presents with dry eyes and dry mouth.
